ssh -i [ssh_key] -p [port_number] cloud@[public_ip_address]

ssh_key: points to the ssh private key file corresponding to the key that was associated while creating the Kubernetes cluster. If no ssh key was provided during Kubernetes cluster creation, use the ssh private key of the management server.
port_number: can be obtained from the Port Forwarding Tab (Public Port column)

message.installwizard.copy.whatisacluste:
A cluster provides a way to group hosts. The hosts in a cluster all have identical hardware, run the same hypervisor, are on the same subnet, and access the same shared storage. Virtual machine instances (VMs) can be live-migrated from one host to another within the same cluster, without interrupting service to the user. A cluster is the third-largest organizational unit within a ABLESTACK™; deployment. Clusters are contained within pods, and pods are contained within zones.

ABLESTACK™; allows multiple clusters in a cloud deployment, but for a Basic Installation, we only need one cluster.
message.installwizard.copy.whatisahost:
A host is a single computer. Hosts provide the computing resources that run the guest virtual machines. Each host has hypervisor software installed on it to manage the guest VMs (except for bare metal hosts, which are a special case discussed in the Advanced Installation Guide). For example, a Linux KVM-enabled server, a Citrix XenServer server, and an ESXi server are hosts. In a Basic Installation, we use a single host running XenServer or KVM.

The host is the smallest organizational unit within a ABLESTACK™; deployment. Hosts are contained within clusters, clusters are contained within pods, and pods are contained within zones.
message.installwizard.copy.whatisapod:
A pod often represents a single rack. Hosts in the same pod are in the same subnet.

A pod is the second-largest organizational unit within a ABLESTACK™; deployment. Pods are contained within zones. Each zone can contain one or more pods; in the Basic Installation, you will have just one pod in your zone.
message.installwizard.copy.whatisazone: A zone is the largest organizational unit within a ABLESTACK™; deployment. A zone typically corresponds to a single datacenter, although it is permissible to have multiple zones in a datacenter. The benefit of organizing infrastructure into zones is to provide physical isolation and redundancy. For example, each zone can have its own power supply and network uplink, and the zones can be widely separated geographically (though this is not required).
message.installwizard.copy.whatiscloudst:
ABLESTACK is a software platform that pools computing resources to build public, private, and hybrid Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) clouds. ABLESTACK manages the Network, storage, and compute nodes that make up a cloud infrastructure. Use ABLESTACK to deploy, manage, and configure cloud computing environments.

Extending beyond individual Instance images running on commodity hardware, ABLESTACK provides a turnkey cloud infrastructure software stack for delivering virtual datacenters as a service - delivering all of the essential components to build, deploy, and manage multi-tier and multi-tenant cloud applications. Both open-source and Premium versions are available, with the open-source version offering nearly identical features.
message.installwizard.copy.whatisprimary:
A ABLESTACK™; cloud infrastructure makes use of two types of storage: primary storage and secondary storage. Both of these can be iSCSI or NFS servers, or localdisk.

Primary storage is associated with a cluster, and it stores the disk volumes of each guest VM for all the VMs running on hosts in that cluster. The primary storage server is typically located close to the hosts.
message.installwizard.copy.whatisseconda:
Secondary storage is associated with a zone, and it stores the following:
  • Templates - OS images that can be used to boot VMs and can include additional configuration information, such as installed applications
  • ISO images - OS images that can be bootable or non-bootable
  • Disk volume snapshots - saved copies of VM data which can be used for data recovery or to create new templates

message.network.offering.mac.address.cha:
Applicable for guest Networks on VMware hypervisor only.
Reject - If the guest OS changes the effective MAC address of the Instance to a value that is different from the MAC address of the Instance Network adapter (set in the .vmx configuration file), the switch drops all inbound frames to the adapter.
If the guest OS changes the effective MAC address of the Instance back to the MAC address of the Instance Network adapter, the virtual machine receives frames again.
Accept - If the guest OS changes the effective MAC address of the virtual machine to a value that is different from the MAC address of the Instance Network adapter, the switch allows frames to the new address to pass.
None - Default to value from global setting.

message.kubernetes.node.drain: Before planned stop, verify the target node, PDB, replicas and spare capacity with kubeconfig, and control AutoScaler reconciliation. Cordon the node, apply the approved LB exclusion policy and complete drain. Do not force past PDB or data-loss warnings. Verify actual external LB, application and data before normal stop.

Keep the node cordoned until cross-node NodePort/Service traffic succeeds. Then verify uncordon, workload readiness, removal of LB exclusion and actual backend recovery, external HTTP and data. This guidance does not automatically drain or guarantee uninterrupted traffic.

message.userdata.clone.intro: Reuse the source name, body and variables to register new data under the same owner. Existing VMs, templates and ISOs are not changed automatically.
message.userdata.clone.policy: Each UUID is an independent immutable version. Change the body and register a new name. Identical bodies under the same owner are rejected even when names or variable declarations differ. There is no update API or automatic version numbering.
message.userdata.clone.apply.vm: Review the source usage tabs first. Explicitly select the new UUID and variable values in each VM user data reset action and check state and reboot requirements. To roll back, select the old UUID and its original variable values. Compare the VM stored body; a reference ID alone does not prove equal content. Previously executed guest script effects need separate recovery.
message.userdata.clone.apply.template: Explicitly link the new UUID with the original policy on each template or ISO. Only subsequently created VMs are affected. To roll back, relink the old UUID and policy. Preserve previous versions until their references are removed.
message.userdata.clone.bom: Registration and cloning preserve BOM, CRLF and binary bytes. Current APPEND merging may not recognize cloud-config starting with a BOM. Use a supported BOM-free format for merging and verify actual VM creation. Choosing plain text editing normalizes line endings to LF.
message.userdata.clone.history.contract: Source metadata is saved as a comment on the new item and displayed here. Comments can be removed or have their visibility changed by authorized users; this is advisory metadata, not an immutable audit log or application history. No parent or ordering is inferred for external API registrations or missing notes. Source notes store only UUIDs and byte counts to fit the annotation API’s 255-character limit. Review names and variables in each version’s details and clone previews.
